title: RGBD20K: A Large-Scale Benchmark for RGB-D Semantic Segmentation
summary: In this paper, we propose RGBD20K, a novel dataset for facilitating the development of more robust and general RGB-D semantic segmentation by encompassing abundant categories and high-quality annotations. RGBD20K possesses several attractive properties: (1) Expanded Semantic Space. In particular, it covers 160 fine-grained categories, largely surpassing the category diversity of existing popular RGB-D benchmarks (e.g., NYUv2 with 40 classes and SUN RGB-D with 37 classes). With such enriched semantic coverage, we expect to promote the learning of more generalizable segmentation models. (2) Larger Scale. Compared with current benchmarks, RGBD20K offers 20,000 RGB-D image pairs, providing a substantially larger training resource that benefits the development of more powerful deep models. (3) High-Fidelity Annotation. We perform rigorous re-evaluation and correction of existing labels to resolve long-standing annotation noise, resulting in a clean and reliable ground-truth foundation. Furthermore, we propose a novel score-purified fusion (SPF) method, which achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in leveraging high-quality multimodal information for RGB-D semantic segmentation. The dataset is here: https://github.com/ShaohuaDong2021/RGBD20K/.

AI.tldr: RGBD20K: a large, 160-category RGB-D dataset with 20k image pairs and cleaned annotations, plus a score-purified fusion method (SPF) achieving state-of-the-art RGB-D semantic segmentation across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Address limited category diversity, scale, and annotation noise in existing RGB-D segmentation benchmarks to enable learning of more generalizable models and to leverage high-quality multimodal information.
AI.method: Dataset construction with 160 fine-grained categories, 20,000 RGB-D pairs, rigorous re-evaluation/correction of labels; proposal of score-purified fusion (SPF) for fusing RGB and depth for segmentation.
AI.result: RGBD20K offers expanded semantic space, larger scale, and high-fidelity annotations; SPF achieves state-of-the-art performance on evaluated benchmarks, demonstrating effective multimodal fusion for RGB-D segmentation.
AI.conclusion: RGBD20K provides a richer, cleaner resource that promotes generalizable RGB-D semantic segmentation; SPF demonstrates the benefit of high-quality multimodal fusion; dataset and method are publicly released.

title: Clinical Knowledge Graphs for Chest X-Ray Device Reasoning
comment: 19 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Post-hoc descriptive analysis on archived RANZCR CLiP test predictions
summary:
Chest radiographs are routinely used to verify the position of catheters, tubes, and other support devices. Existing image models often return labels or segmentations, while report-processing systems structure text without access to image geometry. We present an uncertainty-aware clinical knowledge graph that represents device instances, tip estimates, placement assessments, provenance, report events, and temporal links as separate but connected evidence.
  We evaluate the implemented visual graph layer using saved predictions from the complete RANZCR CLiP test archive, comprising 30,083 studies from 3,255 patients across five non-overlapping outer folds. The graph builder materializes 914,632 B7 evidence nodes and 884,549 typed relationships. All 118,647 B7 predicted-device nodes retain tip covariance, placement probabilities, fragment provenance, and fragment counts, whereas the direct B2 baseline retains none of these fields. We further define typed data contracts, uncertainty representations, abstention rules, report-image grounding, and longitudinal query mechanisms for extending the graph to report-bearing cohorts.
  The reported graph-materialization analysis is post-hoc descriptive and does not establish report grounding, longitudinal performance, or clinical utility. It demonstrates a reproducible foundation for evidence-preserving AI reasoning over chest X-ray device assessments.

AI.tldr: Uncertainty-aware clinical knowledge graph for chest X-ray device assessments; post-hoc graph-materialization on large RANZCR CLiP data showing rich evidence nodes and provenance, but no demonstrated clinical utility.
AI.motivation: Preserve and reason over multi-source evidence (image-derived device data, placement estimates, provenance, and report events) with uncertainty while enabling longitudinal querying and grounding to improve interpretability and traceability.
AI.method: Build a visual graph layer atop predictions; materialize 914,632 B7 evidence nodes and 884,549 typed relationships from the RANZCR CLiP archive (30,083 studies, 3,255 patients). Retain 118,647 B7 predicted-device nodes with tip covariance, placement probabilities, fragment provenance, and fragment counts; compare to a direct B2 baseline that retains none of these fields. Define typed data contracts, uncertainty representations, abstention rules, report-image grounding, and longitudinal query mechanisms for extending the graph to report-bearing cohorts.
AI.result: Post-hoc descriptive graph-materialization analysis; does not establish report grounding, longitudinal performance, or clinical utility. Demonstrates a reproducible foundation for evidence-preserving AI reasoning over chest X-ray device assessments.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers an evidence-preserving, uncertainty-aware graph representation to support future evaluation of grounding, longitudinal performance, and clinical utility in chest radiograph device assessments.

title: World Action Agent: Harnessing VLMs for Robot Manipulation via World Action Rehearsal
summary: General-purpose vision-language models (VLMs) bring broad knowledge and spatial reasoning to robot manipulation, yet existing systems either use them indirectly, to predict constraints or write programs, or give them a view of the scene rather than a world in which to act. We present World Action Agent (WAA), a multi-agent harness through which VLMs pilot robots with basic tools, making every decision within a visual action workspace. The workspace has three properties. Contact views, selected automatically from the scene geometry, present the scene around the current interaction. Action rehearsal turns each action into an editable proposal that the agent, alone or through an Imagination Agent, previews and revises against planning feedback before execution. In-view correction closes the loop between observation, rehearsal, and low-level execution, letting the agent remove residual offsets in the view where it observes them. Through the same workspace, WAA acquires embodied procedural knowledge in two ways: it evolves multimodal skills from expert videos and human teaching under evidence-based review and consults them through a Skill Agent, and its interaction traces train smaller VLMs to pilot the same harness. On LIBERO-Pro, WAA with skills evolved only from LIBERO-90 reaches a state-of-the-art 75.6% average success, outperforming end-to-end VLAs, code-as-policy agents, and a visual-harness baseline with the same backbone; the same skills remain effective on robosuite without further learning. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on harness traces raises its out-of-domain success from 1.7% to 43.3%.

AI.tldr: WAA integrates vision-language models into a visual action workspace for embodied robot manipulation, using Contact views, action rehearsal, and in-view correction, plus Skill and Imagination Agents to evolve and reuse procedural knowledge. It achieves state-of-the-art results on LIBERO-Pro and improves out-of-domain generalization when fine-tuning an LLM on harness traces.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations of existing VLM-based robotic systems that either operate only on scene views or produce constraints, by embedding VLMs in a world-like action workspace that supports planning, rehearsal, and correction.
AI.method: Introduce World Action Agent (WAA) with Contact views selected from scene geometry, Action rehearsal as editable proposals, an Imagination Agent for planning feedback, in-view correction to close perception-action loop, and two learning modes: (i) evolving multimodal skills from expert videos and human teaching via a Skill Agent, with interaction traces training smaller VLM pilots; (ii) training an LLM to pilot the same harness via harness traces. Evaluation on LIBERO-Pro and robosuite; Qwen3.5-9B fine-tuning on harness traces.
AI.result: On LIBERO-Pro, WAA with skills evolved from LIBERO-90 reaches 75.6% average success, outperforming end-to-end VLAs, code-as-policy agents, and a visual-harness baseline; skills transfer to robosuite without further learning. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on harness traces increases out-of-domain success from 1.7% to 43.3%.
AI.conclusion: Embedding VLMs within a structured, interactive action workspace with rehearsal, correction, and skill evolution enables robust embodied manipulation and strong cross-domain transfer, outperforming baselines and enabling improved generalization of base LLMs when trained on harness traces.

title: PUBG Ally: A Conversational Embodied Agent as an AI Teammate
summary: We introduce PUBG Ally, an embodied agent for PUBG: BATTLEGROUNDS that can reason, act autonomously, and play alongside players as a voice-enabled teammate. Building such a teammate requires combining two difficult capabilities: it must perceive and respond to a constantly changing game world under strict latency constraints while interacting naturally with players, keeping its speech synchronized with its actions. Ally therefore combines agentic tool use with real-time game control. A language-model agent uses a controlled interface to inspect game information, interpret player speech, maintain context, decide what to say, and issue high-level action choices that steer a faster control layer for movement, combat, and recovery. Because the player's and Ally's speech and actions continually shape each other and the course of the match, training requires data from actual gameplay. We therefore collect data across nearly 39k sessions in which real players play alongside Ally, recording gameplay, player speech, agent decisions, tool use, actions, and player feedback, and use these records for iterative training. To evaluate teammate quality, we use player feedback and preference comparisons to identify gaps between offline evaluations and player preferences, and iteratively refine the evaluation criteria. Deploying Ally in live service further requires low-latency on-device execution and safeguards for player-facing communication, which we address through model compression, context compaction, targeted safety training, runtime guardrails, and memory redaction. During the live service, we surveyed players in 141 countries. Among respondents whose play with Ally was confirmed in game records, positive responses exceeded negative responses by 25.1 percentage points when asked whether they would recommend Ally, with players describing Ally not only as a tool but also as a teammate or companion.

AI.tldr: A language-model-based embodied agent named PUBG Ally acts as a real-time, voice-enabled teammate in PUBG, using a two-tier architecture: a language-model reasoning agent and a fast control layer for low-latency actions. It learns from nearly 39k live gameplay sessions, optimizes via player feedback, and demonstrates positive reception in live deployment with safeguards and on-device execution.
AI.motivation: To create a responsive, naturalistic teammate for dynamic, latency-sensitive games by integrating perception, language reasoning, and actuation, while ensuring safe, player-aligned interactions.
AI.method: A language-model agent interfaces with game state, interprets player speech, maintains context, decides on spoken responses, and issues high-level actions that guide a fast control layer handling movement, combat, and recovery. Training uses data from ~39k real gameplay sessions, including gameplay, speech, agent decisions, tool use, actions, and feedback. Evaluation combines offline criteria with player preference comparisons, refined iteratively. Live deployment adds low-latency on-device execution and safety measures (compression, context management, targeted safety training, runtime guardrails, memory redaction).
AI.result: User-facing evaluation shows a net positive reception: among players whose play with Ally was confirmed in records, willingness to recommend Ally exceeded unwillingness by 25.1 percentage points. Players described Ally as both a tool and a teammate/companion.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates the feasibility of a two-tier, language-model–driven embodied agent capable of perception, reasoning, and real-time control in a live, latency-constrained game, with iterative evaluation and safety-preserving deployment; it combines data-driven training from large-scale play with on-device optimization to support live service.

title: Qwen-Planner-Agent: A Closed-Loop AI-for-AI Framework for Real-World Mobile Planner Agents
summary: The rapid progression of large language models is extending AI from passive content generation into the active workflows of engineering and scientific discovery. This shift raises a compelling question: can AI be both the object of development and an active participant in building next-generation AI systems? We explore this question by building Qwen-Planner-Agent within a closed-loop AI-for-AI framework for scalable development and iterative improvement. Mobile planning offers a demanding test of this approach: complex, long-horizon tasks challenge agent reliability, while costly real-device interaction limits development scalability. The framework connects data production, model training, and deployment through a shared action-feedback-verification contract. (i) AI for Data builds a human-gated agentic data flywheel in which specialized agents construct tasks, collect interaction trajectories, curate and balance training data, and use training feedback to guide subsequent data generation. (ii) AI for Training combines a supervised planning cold start with hybrid-environment online agentic reinforcement learning, where we introduce Competence-Aware Reward-and-Advantage Engineering (CARE) to reduce reasoning and tool-use costs while preserving task performance. (iii) AI drives model--harness co-evolution through an execution-evidence-driven loop that orchestrates memory, skills, and tools at runtime and feeds structured action feedback and preserved failure traces back into coordinated model and harness adaptation. Qwen-Planner-Agent achieves the best overall performance among all evaluated models and systems on MobilePA-Bench, improving over its base model across tool use, memory, skills, and sub-agent coordination. Further evaluations of our model show improvements across non-mobile agentic benchmarks while largely preserving general capabilities.

AI.tldr: Qwen-Planner-Agent demonstrates a closed-loop AI-for-AI workflow for scalable AI development, introducing a data flywheel, competence-aware training (CARE), and an execution-evidence-driven loop to co-evolve memory, skills, and tools, achieving state-of-the-art results on MobilePA-Bench and improvements on other benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To enable AI to be both the object of development and an active participant in building AI systems, addressing reliability and scalability in AI-assisted engineering and scientific discovery, especially for complex, long-horizon tasks.
AI.method: (i) AI for Data: a human-gated agentic data flywheel that generates tasks, collects trajectories, curates training data, and uses feedback for data generation. (ii) AI for Training: a cold-start supervised planning phase plus hybrid-environment online agentic RL with Competence-Aware Reward-and-Advantage Engineering (CARE) to reduce reasoning/tool-use costs while maintaining task performance. (iii) AI-driven model-harness co-evolution via an execution-evidence-driven loop that manages memory, skills, tools, and preserves failure traces to update both model and harness.
AI.result: Qwen-Planner-Agent achieves the best overall performance among evaluated models/systems on MobilePA-Bench, surpassing its base model in tool use, memory, skills, and sub-agent coordination, with additional boosts on non-mobile agentic benchmarks and largely preserved general capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop AI-for-AI development is feasible and beneficial for scalable, iterative AI system improvement, combining data generation, training, and deployment feedback to drive co-evolution of models and their harnesses.

title: AV-GRPO: Modality-Anchored Decoupling Diffusion Reinforcement Learning for Joint Audio-Video Generation
summary: Recent years have witnessed major progress in joint audio-video generation. Existing models still suffer from limited per-modality fidelity, insufficient text-modality alignment and weak cross-modal synchronization. While reinforcement-learning post-training offers a promising remedy, directly adapting it to joint audio-video generation is challenging. Heterogeneous multimodal rewards entangle learning signals and complicate credit assignment. Joint optimization of two modality towers is computationally expensive given their divergent dynamics. Moreover, synchronization evaluation difficulty depends on paired samples, preventing fair reward comparisons. We propose AV-GRPO, a modality-anchored online diffusion RL framework, and 5DAV, a decoupled, difficulty-controllable training dataset. AV-GRPO includes three key modules: (1) modality-anchored rollouts to disentangle learning signals and stabilize difficulty; (2) trajectory-locked frozen-tower optimization to reduce cost and reassign credit; (3) adaptive objectives and perturbation strengths tailored to modality-specific dynamics. This converts coupled multimodal preference learning into unimodal subproblems for precise reward attribution and better synchronization. Our 5DAV dataset decouples samples across five dimensions for systematic training. Experiments on JavisBench and VABench demonstrate AV-GRPO outperforms LTX-2.3 in generation quality, semantic alignment and cross-modal synchronization under LoRA and full fine-tuning. Ablations confirm our designs. Code and data: https://github.com/zhiyuxu03/AV-GRPO

AI.tldr: AV-GRPO is a modality-anchored online diffusion RL framework for joint audio-video generation, paired with 5DAV, a decoupled, difficulty-controllable dataset. It disentangles learning signals, reduces credit assignment complexity via a frozen-tower trajectory-locked optimization, and uses modality-tailored objectives, yielding improved generation quality, semantic alignment, and cross-modal synchronization over LTX-2.3 on JavisBench/VABench. Code and data available online.
AI.motivation: To address limited per-modality fidelity, weak text-modality alignment, and poor cross-modal synchronization in joint audio-video generation, compounded by the difficulty of applying reinforcement learning due to heterogeneous rewards, credit assignment challenges, costly joint optimization, and evaluation biases tied to paired samples.
AI.method: Introduce AV-GRPO with three modules: (1) modality-anchored rollouts to separate learning signals and stabilize difficulty; (2) trajectory-locked frozen-tower optimization to lower cost and reassign credit; (3) adaptive, modality-specific objectives and perturbation strengths. This converts the coupled multimodal objective into unimodal subproblems for precise reward attribution and better synchronization. Complemented by 5DAV, which decouples samples across five dimensions for systematic training.
AI.result: Empirical results on JavisBench and VABench show AV-GRPO outperforms the prior LTX-2.3 in generation quality, semantic alignment, and cross-modal synchronization under both LoRA and full fine-tuning. Ablation studies validate the design choices.
AI.conclusion: The combination of modality-anchored RL with a decoupled training dataset enables more accurate credit assignment and improved audiovisual synchronization, achieving superior multimodal generation performance; code and data are released.

title: Coding Agents for Generalized Task and Motion Planning Problems
summary: Task and motion planning (TAMP) problems remain difficult even with full observability and object-centric states because discrete decisions are tightly coupled to geometric, kinematic, and dynamic constraints. Generalized TAMP addresses this difficulty by exploiting regularities across problem instances to reduce planning effort on new instances. However, existing methods require substantial TAMP-specific engineering. We investigate whether coding agents can automate this process by synthesizing programs that generalize across instances. Given a task description and simulator access, each agent chooses how to interact with the environment while developing a program within a fixed synthesis budget. The program is then frozen and evaluated on unseen instances. We evaluate Claude Code (Opus 5) and Codex (GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6 Astra) on 28 simulated environments from KinDER and PDDLStream, with object counts beyond those evaluated in the original benchmark. Across all program synthesis methods, we evaluate 980 generated programs on 100 held-out instances each, 98,000 evaluation episodes in total. Overall, we find that coding agents are surprisingly effective at generalized TAMP: all three agent configurations outperform hand-engineered planners, one-shot generation, and an LLM-based generalized planning baseline in mean success (56% to 95% versus 47% for the planners, on the 16 environments where a planner is available). As object counts grow, the agents' programs maintain higher success than the planner, using an order of magnitude less computation per instance on average. Logs show agents using interaction to calibrate physical models, test edge cases, and refine strategies. We release all code, including the full prompts given to the agents. These findings suggest that coding agents are a strong baseline for generalized TAMP.

AI.tldr: Coding agents synthesize generalizable programs for Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) and outperform hand-engineered planners and baselines across KinDER and PDDLStream benchmarks, maintaining higher success with more objects and far lower per-instance computation.
AI.motivation: TAMP is hard due to tight coupling between discrete decisions and geometric/dynamic constraints. Generalized TAMP aims to leverage problem regularities to reduce planning effort, but existing approaches require substantial engineering. The paper investigates whether AI coding agents can automatically synthesize generalizable programs.
AI.method: Agents interact with the environment to develop a program within a fixed synthesis budget, then the program is frozen and evaluated on unseen instances. Evaluations span 28 simulated environments from KinDER and PDDLStream with object counts exceeding prior benchmarks. 980 programs were generated and evaluated across 100 held-out instances each (98,000 episodes total). Three agent configurations were tested: Claude Code (Opus 5), Codex (GPT-5.6 Sol), and GPT-6 Astra. Measures include success rates and computational efficiency.
AI.result: Across all methods, coding agents outperform hand-engineered planners, one-shot generation, and an LLM-based generalized planning baseline in mean success (56%–95% vs 47% for planners on environments where a planner exists). As object counts increase, agents maintain higher success and require an order of magnitude less computation per instance on average. Logs indicate agents use interaction to calibrate physical models, test edge cases, and refine strategies. The authors release all code and prompts.
AI.conclusion: Coding agents constitute a strong baseline for generalized TAMP, capable of generalizing across instances with significantly reduced engineering and computational costs. The approach shows robust performance gains and supports broader applicability to generalized planning in TAMP.

title: RAPID: Robot Agentic Programming from Demonstrations
summary: Coding agents have demonstrated enormous success in solving complex programming problems. To leverage their potential for robot systems, this work introduces Robot Agentic Programming from Demonstrations (RAPID), which automatically generates, verifies, and refines robot programs, given a single visual human demonstration. The iterative agentic loop of code refinement requires several key ingredients: (i) a testable task specification, (ii) action primitives for robot execution, and (iii) an interactive environment for program execution and verification. RAPID infers all three from the demonstration automatically. To make the resulting program reusable beyond the demonstration setting, RAPID uses an object-centric relational program representation that focuses on the underlying structure of the demonstrated strategy rather than the specific motion per se: it expresses the action primitives as trajectory-optimization programs that realize object-level motion effects, while composing them through relational constraints that capture scene-specific geometry at run time. We evaluated RAPID in simulation on eight challenging contact-rich nonprehensile manipulation tasks as well as general prehensile manipulation tasks in the LIBERO-Pro benchmark. We also successfully deployed it on a real Franka arm and evaluated on all eight nonprehensile tasks. In all experiments, RAPID demonstrated strong performance, with generalization over object pose, shape, material, and environment. Website: https://yuyaoliu.me/projects/rapid.

AI.tldr: RAPID automatically derives reusable robot programs from a single visual demonstration by inferring a task spec, action primitives, and an execution environment, using an object-centric relational representation and trajectory-optimization primitives; it generalizes to varied objects and is validated in simulation and on a real arm.
AI.motivation: Reduce manual programming for robot manipulation by converting demonstrations into verifiable, reusable programs that generalize across object properties and scenes.
AI.method: From one demonstration, RAPID infers: a testable task specification; action primitives for execution; an interactive verification environment. Represents programs relationally and object-centrically, with trajectory-optimization motion primitives and scene-aware constraints; evaluations in LIBERO-Pro and a real Franka arm.
AI.result: Strong generalization across pose, shape, material, environment; success on eight nonprehensile tasks plus prehensile tasks; successful real-robot deployment on all eight nonprehensile tasks.
AI.conclusion: RAPID demonstrates automatic code-like robot programming from demonstrations, enabling reusable, verified, and generalizable robot programs; supports scalable deployment in real-world manipulation tasks.

title: DeltaWAM: Delta World Action Models for Bimanual Manipulation
summary: World-action models (WAMs) transfer visual and motion priors from pretrained video generators to robot control by jointly modeling visual dynamics and actions. Existing WAMs, however, predict dense future frames during training, repeatedly modeling largely unchanged content and coupling action-conditioned dynamics to nuisance appearance variations. At inference, processing each complete observation with the heavy video expert bottlenecks few-step action generation. Accordingly, we propose DeltaWAM, which jointly predicts visual deltas and actions using dense-anchor, sparse-delta, and action streams, with three architectures that differ in representation and computation sharing. We further develop Streaming Delta Memory (SDM), which updates cached anchor context with compact observed deltas, reducing heavy video-expert processing. On RoboTwin, DeltaWAM with SDM improves average success over Fast-WAM from 81.3% to 85.4% in the clean setting and from 75.8% to 83.9% under visual randomization. The three architectures reduce training FLOPs by 17.78-23.77%, while SDM reduces one-step inference latency and FLOPs by 36.57% and 31.55%, respectively; real-world evaluations further show the highest overall success rate and normalized progress among the evaluated policies. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/DeltaWAM. Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/DeltaWAM.

AI.tldr: DeltaWAM introduces dense-anchor, sparse-delta, and action streams to predict visual deltas with a streaming delta memory (SDM) for efficiency, achieving better RoboTwin performance and lower training/inference costs with three architectures.
AI.motivation: Existing world-action models (WAMs) rely on dense future-frame prediction, which wastes compute on largely static content and bottlenecks inference with heavy video-experts. A more efficient, delta-based, streaming approach is needed to transfer visual/motion priors to robot control.
AI.method: DeltaWAM jointly predicts visual deltas and actions using three architectures (dense-anchor, sparse-delta, action streams). It introduces Streaming Delta Memory (SDM) to update cached anchor context with compact observed deltas, reducing heavy video-expert processing. The approach also evaluates on RoboTwin with performance and FLOPs metrics.
AI.result: On RoboTwin, DeltaWAM with SDM improves average success from 81.3% (Fast-WAM) to 85.4% in the clean setting and from 75.8% to 83.9% under visual randomization. Training FLOPs are reduced by 17.78-23.77%, and one-step inference latency and FLOPs are reduced by 36.57% and 31.55%, respectively. Real-world evaluations show the highest overall success rate and normalized progress among evaluated policies.
AI.conclusion: DeltaWAM with SDM provides more efficient, competitive WAMs that better leverage visual dynamics and actions for robot control, maintaining or improving performance while reducing compute. Code and a project website are provided.

title: Style, Not Self: Surface Cues Explain Zero-Shot Code Attribution by Large Language Models
summary: If a language model can recognize code it wrote, it may favor that code as a judge, and instances of one model monitoring each other could collude. We test this zero-shot on current commercial models. Five LLMs generate solutions to MBPP, HumanEval, and DS-1000, seven more to MBPP, and models act as evaluators in four tasks: picking their own solution from a pair, judging whether a single solution is their own, identifying which of two solutions a named model wrote, and judging quality blind. In the single-solution task, balanced accuracy is 49-58% for all 15 model-benchmark combinations, while raw accuracy (38-67%) mostly reflects how readily a model claims authorship. In the pairwise task, accuracy across 14 evaluator-opponent combinations correlates at r=0.93 with how often the evaluator's solution is longer. Attribution to a named model succeeds on some pairs and is consistently inverted on others. A rule-based normalization that strips docstrings, comments, type hints, and local names preserves Pass@1 and leaves ten of twelve re-tested results at chance; the other two follow a length difference it leaves, although a trained classifier still separates most normalized pairs. Claude Haiku's self-preference also disappears. We recommend reporting balanced accuracy, heuristic baselines, and label consistency.

AI.tldr: Zero-shot experiments show LLMs can monitor and attribute authorship of code but with limited accuracy; length and self-authorship bias largely drive judgments; normalization reduces signal, yet some results persist; findings advocate reporting balanced accuracy, baselines, and label consistency rather than raw accuracy.
AI.motivation: Assess whether language models can recognize code they authored or monitor other models, and whether self-assessments can lead to collusion or biased evaluation.
AI.method: Multiple LLMs generated coding solutions for MBPP, HumanEval, and DS-1000; several more solved MBPP; models also acted as evaluators across four tasks: (i) select best among a pair, (ii) judge if a single solution is their own, (iii) identify which named model wrote a solution, (iv) judge quality blind. Metrics include balanced accuracy and raw accuracy; normalization by stripping docstrings/comments/type hints/local names; a trained classifier distinguishes normalized pairs; Pass@1 examined; Claude Haiku's self-preference observed.
AI.result: In single-solution tasks, balanced accuracy ranges 49-58% across 15 model-benchmark pairs; raw accuracy 38-67% largely tracks authorship claims. In pairwise tasks, evaluator-vs-opponent accuracy correlates r=0.93 with relative solution length. Attribution to a named model is successful on some pairs but inverted on others. Rule-based normalization preserves Pass@1 and leaves ten of twelve re-tested results at chance; two remaining results align with post-normalization length differences. A trained classifier still separates most normalized pairs. Claude Haiku’s self-preference disappears after normalization.
AI.conclusion: Self-authorship signals exist but are fragile, often confounded by length and heuristics. Normalization can remove much of the signal, underscoring the need for robust baselines and reporting practices. The authors recommend reporting balanced accuracy, heuristic baselines, and label consistency rather than raw or sole attribution metrics.

title: AD-WM: Action-Discriminative World Models for Counterfactual Model Predictive Control
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Project page: https://ad-wm.github.io/
summary: Latent world models are typically trained to predict factual transitions, whereas model predictive control (MPC) must compare alternative actions from the same state. A model can therefore achieve low factual prediction error yet poorly distinguish candidate actions. We introduce AD-WM, an action-discriminative joint-embedding world model for counterfactual MPC. AD-WM combines residual latent dynamics with predictor-level action-recovery regularization, using inverse dynamics and a normalized recovery objective motivated by conditional mutual information. Both objectives encourage planning transitions to preserve action information; their auxiliary heads are discarded at test time, leaving MPC unchanged. On OGBench-Cube, AD-WM improves hard-start success from 3.7% to 52.0% over a matched LeWM baseline and improves mean success over the reproduced baseline in four of five simulation environments. Planning diagnostics show that factual prediction error and whole-bank action ranking do not follow the closed-loop success ordering, whereas CEM-aligned elite regret tracks success more closely. With a frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder and matched DROID post-training, AD-WM also improves zero-shot transfer to our Franka setup, increasing basic pick-and-place success from 42.2% to 71.1% without lab-specific adaptation. These results suggest that world models for planning should preserve action-dependent differences needed for counterfactual selection, rather than optimize factual prediction accuracy alone. More videos and code are available at https://ad-wm.github.io/.

AI.tldr: AD-WM promotes action-discriminative latent world models for counterfactual MPC by coupling residual dynamics with action-recovery regularization; test-time MPC remains unchanged, but planning quality improves and transfers well.
AI.motivation: Factual-prediction accuracy alone does not guarantee good action discrimination for counterfactual planning. Planning requires preserving action-dependent information in latent representations, which standard world models may discard.
AI.method: Train an action-discriminative joint-embedding world model (AD-WM) using residual latent dynamics and predictor-level action-recovery regularization via inverse dynamics and a normalized recovery objective inspired by conditional mutual information. Auxiliary heads are used during training but discarded at test time, keeping MPC unchanged.
AI.result: In OGBench-Cube, hard-start success rises from 3.7% to 52.0% over a matched LeWM baseline; mean success improves in four of five environments. Planning diagnostics reveal that factual error and whole-bank action ranking do not align with closed-loop success, while CEM-aligned elite regret tracks success more closely. With frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder and matched DROID post-training, zero-shot transfer to Franka improves basic pick-and-place success from 42.2% to 71.1% without task-specific adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Planning-oriented world models should preserve action-dependent differences for counterfactual selection, not just minimize factual prediction error. AD-WM provides substantial gains and shows promising transfer, underscoring the importance of action-aware representations in MPC.

title: Jev-Mobile: Jev as an Executor for Mobile GUI Agents
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have become a common foundation for autonomous mobile GUI agents, but most existing systems rely on the VLM for both planning and action grounding at nearly every interaction step, leading to substantial latency and model-serving cost. We introduce Jev-Mobile, which shifts this paradigm to low-frequency VLM planning and high-frequency lightweight execution: the VLM specifies local goals, the accessibility tree defines a structured executable action space, and Jev, a fast typed decision model, repeatedly selects actions within this space. This design allows multiple GUI actions to be executed under a single VLM decision, reducing expensive VLM inference while preserving adaptive interaction. On the full AndroidWorld task suite, Jev-Mobile achieves 79% task success, compared with 78% for SeeAct-V and 84% for a Step-wise VLM baseline. Among successful trajectories, it reduces mean end-to-end execution time by 32.7% and mean model API cost by 73.4% relative to Step-wise VLM. These results show that decoupling high-level VLM reasoning from low-level action execution can substantially improve mobile GUI agent efficiency while maintaining competitive task performance.

AI.tldr: Jev-Mobile decouples high-level planning from low-level GUI actions by using a VLM for infrequent planning and a fast typed decision model (Jev) to execute actions within a structured action space defined by an accessibility tree, reducing VLM latency and API costs while maintaining competitive task success.
AI.motivation: Mitigate the high latency and cost of using large vision-language models for every interaction step in mobile GUI agents by separating planning from execution and by leveraging a structured action space for fast local decision-making.
AI.method: Introduce Jev-Mobile architecture: a VLM provides local goals at low frequency; an accessibility tree defines a structured executable action space; Jev, a fast typed decision model, repeatedly selects actions within this space; enables multiple GUI actions per VLM decision to reduce VLM calls.
AI.result: On AndroidWorld, Jev-Mobile achieves 79% task success (vs 78% SeeAct-V; 84% Step-wise VLM). Among successful trajectories, end-to-end execution time is reduced by 32.7% and mean model API cost by 73.4% compared with Step-wise VLM.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling high-level VLM reasoning from low-level action execution can substantially improve mobile GUI agent efficiency while maintaining competitive task performance.

title: ExplorationBench: Measuring AI Systems' Exploration in Verifiable Alien Worlds
summary: Scientific discovery begins where known problems end. There, AI systems must engage in exploration: framing hypotheses, designing experiments, and iterating on the results. However, evaluating this ability is difficult: (1) how to verify whether a genuinely new hypothesis holds, and (2) how to determine whether a system has discovered it through exploration or merely recalled related knowledge from pre-training data. To this end, we introduce ExplorationBench, which turns the wicked problem of evaluating scientific exploration into a concrete and tractable framework built on verifiable Alien Worlds: their rules are executable, so every answer can be checked exactly, and they conflict with familiar knowledge, so recall alone cannot solve the tasks. The benchmark contains two sandboxes, AlienCode (31 discovery targets, 70 tasks) and AlienLogic (24 discovery targets, 70 tasks). Each sandbox provides a flawed manual, task-specific environmental feedback, and a dedicated tool-call schema. Systems use these resources to explore the sandbox, then solve held-out tasks. We evaluate 10 AI systems and find that the strongest systems can acquire and apply unfamiliar rules, while performance varies substantially across trajectories and continued exploration can stall or reverse earlier gains. ExplorationBench represents a step towards AI systems that can acquire and apply genuinely new knowledge through exploration in unknown environments.

AI.tldr: Introduces ExplorationBench with executable Alien Worlds sandboxes to evaluate whether AI systems can discover genuinely new hypotheses through exploratory reasoning, not just recall; findings show variable trajectories and potential for improvement or regress with continued exploration.
AI.motivation: To address the difficulty of verifying genuinely new hypotheses and distinguishing exploration-driven discovery from recall of pretraining data; requires verifiable, executable environments where new rules can conflict with familiar knowledge.
AI.method: Two sandboxes, AlienCode (31 discovery targets, 70 tasks) and AlienLogic (24 discovery targets, 70 tasks). Each provides a flawed manual, task-specific environmental feedback, and a dedicated tool-call schema. Systems explore the sandbox and then solve held-out tasks. Evaluation spans 10 AI systems.
AI.result: Strongest systems can acquire and apply unfamiliar rules; performance varies across exploration trajectories; continued exploration can stall or even reverse earlier gains.
AI.conclusion: ExplorationBench advances evaluation of genuinely new knowledge acquisition via exploration in unknown environments and highlights both potential and challenges in scalable, verifiable scientific exploration by AI.

title: WanPE: Towards Cinematic Prompt Enhancement for Modern Text-to-Video Generation
summary: Video generation begins in text space by authoring a cinematic screenplay, then materializes into pixels. As contemporary video generators scale to 30 seconds and faithfully follow complex conditions, the textual prompt largely directs the production, planning how actions, camera trajectories, lighting, and sound unfold across multi-shot sequences. In this paper, we present WanPE, a 397B-parameter prompt enhancement model trained on 1.05M real-world videos to master director-level cinematic planning. WanPE formulates shot-level cinematic plans via video-grounded reverse construction and employs Semantic-Consistency GRPO (SC-GRPO) to faithfully preserve user requirements across shots and over time. To benchmark this capability, we curate WanPEval, a human-annotated testbed covering durations from 5 to 30 seconds across varying intent granularities, supported by approximately 11K blind pairwise assessments. When powering Wan3.0's video generator, WanPE-397B boosts human preference over raw user prompts by 10.66-18.84 points at 5-15 seconds and by a dramatic 50.86 points in the 30-second arena. Ablation studies show that reverse construction demonstrates clear superiority over forward rewriting, while SC-GRPO robustly preserves semantic fidelity across model scales. Ultimately, WanPE leads all evaluated commercial offerings at 5-15 seconds and remains competitive with Seedance 2.5 at 30 seconds.

AI.tldr: WanPE is a 397B prompt-enhancement model that enables director-level cinematic planning for video generation, using video-grounded reverse construction and SC-GRPO. It improves user-prompt fidelity and outperforms benchmarks on WanPEval, especially at shorter durations.
AI.motivation: As video generation scales to longer durations and complex multi-shot planning, prompts alone struggle to reliably enforce actions, camera trajectories, lighting, and sound across shots. WanPE aims to elevate prompt-to-video planning to a director-level capability.
AI.method: Train a 397B WanPE on 1.05M real-world videos to learn shot-level planning. Introduce video-grounded reverse construction for shot-level plans and Semantic-Consistency GRPO (SC-GRPO) to preserve user requirements semantically across shots/time. Create WanPEval, a 11K-assessment testbed across 5–30s. Integrate WanPE into Wan3.0 video generator; perform ablations comparing reverse construction vs forward rewriting and testing SC-GRPO across scales. Benchmark against commercial tools and Seedance 2.5.
AI.result: WanPE-397B improves human preference by 10.66–18.84 points at 5–15s, and by 50.86 points at 30s. Reverse construction outperforms forward rewriting; SC-GRPO maintains semantic fidelity across model scales. WanPE leads all evaluated commercial offerings at 5–15s and competes with Seedance 2.5 at 30s.
AI.conclusion: WanPE advances practical, director-level planning for video generation by combining reverse construction with a semantic-consistency objective, yielding substantial preference gains and robust fidelity across durations; it sets a strong benchmark against commercial systems.

title: Pistis Technical Report
summary: We introduce the Pistis model family, comprising 27B- and 9B-parameter multimodal large language models built on Qwen3.6 and Qwen3.5, respectively, and developed through a general and scalable post-training framework. The framework first establishes a strong foundation through large-scale multimodal supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Building on this SFT foundation, we propose Interleaved Distillation and Reinforcement Learning (IDRL), a novel post-training paradigm that tightly integrates on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning within a single training loop. By alternating between the two objectives, rather than optimizing either in isolation or combining them in a static joint loss, IDRL enables more effective knowledge transfer, greater optimization stability, and more precise credit assignment for long-horizon agentic trajectories, leading to stronger performance while mitigating common capability trade-offs. At both model scales, the framework produces two specialized variants: Pistis-Thinking, designed to strengthen deep multimodal reasoning, and Pistis-Agentic, which additionally incorporates agentic trajectory data to support long-horizon planning, iterative reasoning, and tool use. Pistis-Agentic is particularly strong in multimodal search. Both scales outperform their corresponding base models. Beyond model-parameter optimization, we further introduce Pistis-Auto-Harnessing (PAH), a system-level method that automatically improves the agent's inference harness through iterative optimization. Experiments demonstrate that PAH enhances the model performance without updating the model parameters or increasing the interaction budget.

AI.tldr: Pistis introduces 27B- and 9B-parameter multimodal LLMs built on Qwen variants, with a novel Interleaved Distillation and Reinforcement Learning (IDRL) post-training loop, yielding Pistis-Thinking and Pistis-Agentic specializations; adds Pistis-Auto-Harnessing (PAH) system-level optimization that improves inference without updating model parameters. Both scales outperform base models, with Pistis-Agentic excelling in multimodal search and PAH enhancing performance on the inference harness.
AI.motivation: Improve multimodal LLM capabilities through scalable, unified post-training that combines distillation and reinforcement learning in a single loop, and to extend beyond-model improvements via system-level harnessing. Address long-horizon agentic tasks, robust reasoning, tool use, and trade-offs between capabilities.
AI.method: 1) Large-scale multimodal supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to establish a strong foundation. 2) Interleaved Distillation and Reinforcement Learning (IDRL): alternating on-policy distillation and RL within one loop for better credit assignment and stability. 3) Specializations: Pistis-Thinking for deep multimodal reasoning; Pistis-Agentic for long-horizon planning with agentic trajectories and tool use. 4) Pistis-Auto-Harnessing (PAH): system-level method to optimize the inference harness without updating model parameters or increasing interaction budget.
AI.result: Empirical results show both Pistis scales outperform their base models. Pistis-Agentic excels in multimodal search; Pistis-Thinking enhances deep multimodal reasoning. PAH improves performance without parameter updates or extra interaction budget.
AI.conclusion: The IDRL framework yields stronger performance and better knowledge transfer with greater optimization stability and precise credit assignment for long-horizon tasks. Combined with PAH, Pistis achieves system-level gains, yielding robust, scalable multimodal LLMs with specialized agentic and reasoning capabilities.

title: Training Object Permanence in World Models
comment: 26 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables. Project page: https://object-permanence.world
summary: Object permanence and solidity are hallmarks of human cognitive priors. Recent studies show that video generation models, a paradigmatic class of current world models, have begun to show emerged reasoning abilities, making them ideal candidates for building human-like physical intelligence. Do video models have emerged object permanence in them? If not, could we train them with a core-cognition inspired dataset? We introduce WROP (World Reasoning with Object Permanence), a data infrastructure of 150 hand-designed cognitive science inspired tasks, divided into six cognitive categories. We build Blender generators that randomize speed, lighting, camera angle, and other nuisance parameters while preserving each task's cognitive structure, yielding 10,000+ samples per task. We release a 1.5M-sample training corpus and a 300-question exam. On this exam we evaluate 14 video models: 3 reference-to-video, 7 edit, and 4 continuation, among which PWM-WROP, our 16B world model. In a blind pairwise Elo study, PWM-WROP ranks first among continuation models and third overall, behind only a statistical tie between two reference-to-video models. We release the data, exam, model answers, scores, weights, and PWM, our native-PyTorch training stack on AWS Trainium2.

AI.tldr: WROP introduces a core-cognition-inspired synthetic data suite to probe object permanence and solidity in video-generation models; 150 tasks across six cognitive categories, 1.5M training samples, and a 300-question exam to evaluate 14 models, with PWM-WROP (16B) achieving top performance among continuation models and strong overall ranking, followed by releasing data and tools.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether current video-generation models exhibit object permanence and physical priors; address the gap by a curated dataset inspired by cognitive science to train and evaluate models on persistent object understanding.
AI.method: Construct Blender-based data pipelines that randomize nuisance factors (speed, lighting, camera angle) while preserving the cognitive task structure; design 150 tasks in six categories; generate 10k+ samples per task; assemble 1.5M training samples; create 300-question exam; evaluate 14 video models across three archetypes: reference-to-video, edit, continuation; propose PWM-WROP (16B parameter) as world model; training stack on AWS Trainium2.
AI.result: On a blind Elo pairwise evaluation, PWM-WROP ranks first among continuation models and third overall (tied with two reference-to-video models). Data, exam, model answers, scores, weights, and PWM tooling released.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the viability of core-cognition-inspired synthetic data to probe and train video-language-physical priors; provides a reproducible bench and tools; suggests future work to test generalization to real-world video, expand tasks, perform ablations, and study cross-domain transfer.

title: DEEPO: Dual-Entropy Enhanced Policy Optimization for Hallucination in MLLMs
summary:
Reinforcement learning (RL) is widely used to sharpen reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs), yet its effect on hallucination is uneven. We trace this to two weak points in the \emph{correction chain} from reward to parameter update. At the rollout level, hard queries---those with high semantic entropy---frequently produce unanimously wrong sample groups, collapsing the group-relative
  advantage to zero exactly where hallucination risk is highest. At the optimization level, confident-but-wrong tokens are gradient-invisible: a categorical policy's expected score-gradient norm vanishes as its distribution sharpens, so the predictions that most need correction receive the weakest updates. We propose Dual-Entropy Enhanced Policy Optimization (DEEPO), a dual-stage enhancement combining signal
  variance regularization with gradient preconditioning: semantic-entropy-triggered expert prefixes inject grounded continuations on high-uncertainty queries, providing direct supervision and restoring advantage variance, while advantage-sign-aware Renyi preconditioning counteracts logit-level saturation so correction reaches confident errors in the operational confidence regime. Both branches improve over GRPO individually; their interaction is statistically significant on VideoMMMU---the most complex long-horizon task in our evaluation suite (+4.0$, 95\% CI [1.1, 6.9])---and additive elsewhere. DEEPO reduces hallucination while preserving accuracy and training stability.

AI.tldr: A dual-stage enhancement (DEEPO) for RL-based policy optimization in multimodal LLMs; it mitigates hallucination by addressing rollout and optimization bottlenecks via semantic-entropy-triggered expert prefixes and Renyi gradient preconditioning, yielding reduced hallucination while preserving accuracy; shows significant gains on VideoMMMU (+4.0, 95% CI [1.1, 6.9]).
AI.motivation: Hallucination in RL for MLLMs arises from two weak points in the correction chain: (i) rollout-level hard queries produce unanimously wrong sample groups, erasing group-relative advantages; (ii) optimization-level confident-but-wrong tokens have vanishing gradient as the policy sharpens, so corrections are weak where most needed.
AI.method: DEEPO combines two strategies: (1) semantic-entropy-triggered expert prefixes that inject grounded continuations on high-uncertainty queries to restore advantage variance; (2) advantage-sign-aware Renyi preconditioning to counteract logit-level saturation and ensure corrections reach confident errors.
AI.result: Each branch improves over GRPO; combined interaction yields statistically significant improvement on VideoMMMU; reported gain +4.0 with 95% CI [1.1, 6.9]; gains are additive on other tasks; overall reduction in hallucination with preserved accuracy and training stability.
AI.conclusion: DEEPO successfully reduces hallucination while maintaining accuracy and stability; the two components complement each other and may generalize to long-horizon tasks.

title: When Can Agents Forget Their Reasoning? ICLR for Long-Horizon Agent Context Compression
summary: Long horizon language model agents continually accumulate reasoning history, increasing context length and inference cost even after earlier decisions have been executed and observed. Unlike static Chain of Thought compression, removing historical reasoning can change future actions and the resulting interaction trajectory. We study when such reasoning can be safely forgotten. We propose Interaction Aware Compression for Long Horizon Reasoning (ICLR), a training free online method that ranks reasoning blocks using frozen proxy entropy while preserving actions, tool calls, and observations. On 260 WorkBuddyBench tasks, ICLR improves average reward from 0.699 to 0.718, while reducing input, output, and cache read tokens by 25.5%, 14.4%, and 33.3%, respectively. Ablations reveal trajectory amplification, where local reasoning deletion produces nonlinear changes in total computation by altering subsequent interaction. Representation probing, activation patching, and controlled trajectory analyses further suggest that historical reasoning becomes more replaceable once task relevant derived state has been reliably externalized into code, files, tool outputs, or environmental feedback. These results characterize agent reasoning as dynamic working state rather than permanent interaction history.

AI.tldr: ICLR is a training-free online compression that ranks and forgets parts of long-horizon reasoning using frozen proxy entropy, preserving actions and observations; it improves reward slightly and reduces token use.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate reasoning histories that inflate context length and inference cost. Forgetting history could save resources but may alter future trajectories; understanding when safe to forget and how to compress is crucial for scalable, interactive agents.
AI.method: ICLR ranks reasoning blocks online using frozen proxy entropy to decide which reasoning to retain or discard, while ensuring actions, tool calls, and observations remain intact. It is training-free and operates during interaction to compress history without altering the observed interactions.
AI.result: On 260 WorkBuddyBench tasks, average reward rose from 0.699 to 0.718. Token savings: input tokens −25.5%, output tokens −14.4%, cache reads −33.3%. Ablations reveal trajectory amplification: deleting local reasoning can nonlinearly affect subsequent computation. Probing and controlled analyses indicate that historical reasoning becomes replaceable once the derived state is externalized into code, files, tool outputs, or environmental feedback.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning in long-horizon agents acts as dynamic working state rather than permanent history. Safe forgetting is enabled when task-relevant state is externalized, enabling memory compression without harming, and often improving, interaction trajectories.

title: RECLAIM: Can Agents Reproduce the Claims of Machine Learning Papers?
summary: Reproducing a machine learning paper involves most research steps, from installing software and debugging to running experiments, work that AI agents increasingly do. We introduce RECLAIM, a benchmark of 100 NeurIPS 2025 papers that can be rebuilt yearly from new conferences. For each paper we fix in advance the result to reproduce, what counts as a successful reproduction, and a GPU-hour budget. An agent must reproduce that result using the paper and whatever its authors released. What the authors released decides the difficulty tier. Run-tier releases include code, data, and weights; Retrain-tier releases lack weights, so the agent trains the model; Reimplement-tier releases lack code, so the agent writes it. A separate language model grades runs from logs and outputs rather than agents' reports. We run four agents once per paper; the best agent in each tier reproduces only 41% of Run-tier papers, 27% at Retrain, and 15% at Reimplement, where every agent does worst. Failed attempts use on average 29% of their budget, so most stop with budget left. The most common agent error is writing the method without checking any part against the paper's numbers, in 63 of 400 runs.

AI.tldr: RECLAIM is a benchmark of 100 NeurIPS 2025 papers to be rebuilt yearly, with fixed results and tiered releases, to evaluate automated reproduction by agents under GPU-hour budgets.
AI.motivation: To systematically measure and accelerate reproducibility in ML research by providing a benchmark and staged access to code, data, and models, plus automated evaluation.
AI.method: Select 100 papers; fix a target reproduction result; define Run-tier/Retrain-tier/Reimplement-tier releases; run four agents per paper; use a separate language model to grade runs; measure success rates and budget usage; report common failure modes.
AI.result: Best agent reproduces 41% of Run-tier, 27% of Retrain-tier, and 15% of Reimplement-tier papers; failed attempts use ~29% of budget; average common error is implementing the method without validating against paper numbers (63 of 400 runs).
AI.conclusion: Reproducibility remains challenging, especially with limited access to code and data; progress requires robust verification against paper claims and improved tooling for automating checks and sanity tests; budget discipline and error analysis are essential for meaningful benchmarking.

title: Forecast-Dojo: Replayable Environments for Benchmarking and Training LLM Forecasting Agents
summary: We introduce Forecast-Dojo, a replayable environment for benchmarking and training LLM forecasting agents. It combines resolved prediction-market questions with dated news, allowing agents to research an event and revisit their predictions at successive historical dates. The same tasks and tools support repeated evaluation, collection of training interactions, and feedback from recorded outcomes without waiting for new events to resolve. Forecast-Dojo contains 1,568 Polymarket events, split by time into training and evaluation periods, and 18.8M dated news articles. In an evaluation of 12 models, research tools lower Brier score for all 12. Forecasts also improve as events unfold, with the largest gains at steps where more newly dated evidence is recorded. Every model still trails historical market forecasts in both Brier score and accuracy. A belief notebook carried between dates lowers research cost but does not consistently improve forecast quality. Beyond evaluation, Forecast-Dojo provides interaction trajectories and outcome feedback for agent learning, with supervised fine-tuning as a proof of concept.

AI.tldr: Forecast-Dojo: a replayable, historical-evidence-based environment for benchmarking and training LLM forecasting agents using dated news and resolved prediction-market events; demonstrates improved Brier scores with research tools but still lags behind historical market forecasts; includes 1,568 events and 18.8M news articles; supports repeated evaluation and supervised fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Enable reproducible benchmarking and training of LLM forecast agents by combining resolved market questions with dated news to allow retrodictive research and iterative evaluation without waiting for events to resolve.
AI.method: Assemble dataset of Polymarket events with chronological news; enable replay of event history, allow research interactions, measure Brier score and accuracy; evaluate 12 models; include belief notebook; provide agent-learning feedback via interaction trajectories; proof-of-concept supervised fine-tuning.
AI.result: Research tools lower Brier score across all models; forecasts improve as events unfold; largest gains when new dated evidence appears; all models still behind historical market forecasts; belief notebook reduces research cost but doesn't consistently improve forecast quality; environment enables learning and evaluation with outcome feedback.
AI.conclusion: Forecast-Dojo is a valuable benchmark and learning platform for LLM forecasting, enabling repeated evaluation and learning from outcomes, but market forecasts remain superior; further work could explore mechanisms to close gaps and enhance learning signals.

title: SLCA-GRPO: Resolving Cross-Segment Credit Misattribution in Tool-Calling RL
summary: Tool-calling agents produce heterogeneous outputs, interleaving structured tool invocations with user-facing natural language summaries. This output heterogeneity presents a structural failure mode in standard on-policy Reinforcement Learning (RL): algorithms like GRPO indiscriminately broadcast a homogeneous trajectory-level scalar advantage to all tokens. Consequently, gradient noise from summary generation leaks into tool-decision tokens, causing cross-segment credit misattribution and brittle optimization. In this work, we propose SLCA-GRPO, a framework incorporating Segment-Locked Credit Assignment (SLCA). To enable scalable exploration without costly real APIs and stable training, we first construct the Schema-Guided LLM Simulator (SGLS) as foundational training infrastructure. Building on this, SLCA decouples advantage estimation at the structural segment level within a single group of rollouts, without requiring additional rollouts from intermediate states. Supported by Hierarchical Rewards (HierR), SLCA routes execution advantages to tool tokens and preference advantages to summary tokens, eliminating advantage contamination (the dominant cross-segment credit misattribution channel) within each policy update. On a 7B backbone, SLCA-GRPO accelerates convergence and outperforms standard GRPO, ToolPO, and RLTR by +2.53 pp on in-domain evaluation, +1.36 pp on the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard (BFCL), and +9.15 pp on $τ^2$-Bench under the same training budgets, achieving higher accuracy with reduced tool redundancy and costs.

AI.tldr: Proposes Segment-Locked Credit Assignment (SLCA) within GRPO to handle heterogeneous tool-calling outputs; introduces SGLS training simulator and Hierarchical Rewards (HierR) to route segment-specific advantages, achieving faster convergence and higher accuracy on multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Output heterogeneity in tool-calling agents leads to cross-segment credit misattribution as trajectory-level scalar advantages contaminate tool and summary tokens; existing on-policy RL struggles with gradient noise and costly real APIs, necessitating scalable, stable segment-level credit assignment.
AI.method: SLCA-GRPO framework with Schema-Guided LLM Simulator (SGLS) for scalable training; decouples advantage estimation at the structural segment level within a single rollout group; uses HierR to route execution advantages to tool tokens and preference advantages to summary tokens without extra rollouts.
AI.result: Faster convergence and superior performance compared with GRPO, ToolPO, and RLTR: +2.53 percentage points in-domain, +1.36 pp on BFCL, and +9.15 pp on τ^2-Bench under the same training budgets; also achieves higher accuracy with reduced tool redundancy and costs.
AI.conclusion: SLCA-GRPO with SGLS and HierR yields improved credit attribution, stable training, and enhanced performance in tool-calling RL, with potential for broader applicability to structured-output RL settings.

title: A Rapid Pipeline for Training and Deploying ML Models on WeBe Band
summary:
Developing optimized machine-learning algorithms for edge devices with limited computational and memory resources is challenging, time-consuming, and highly dependent on device-specific constraints. In this work, we streamline an edge ML workflow to enable rapid development, optimization, and deployment of machine-learning (ML) models directly on the WeBe Band, a wrist-worn wearable device designed for multimodal physiological data monitoring. The proposed system automatically generates hardware-efficient ML models that can be easily integrated into the WeBe core firmware, supporting AutoML, hardware-aware quantization, and performance profiling to build models that meet desired latency targets while remaining compatible with device memory and power limitations.
  The proposed framework tightly integrates the open-source Piccolo AI ecosystem with an automated pipeline that generates deployable firmware artifacts, performs hardware-aware model compilation, and supports over-the-air (OTA) deployment. The system supports multiple lightweight model classes, including classical machine-learning algorithms and neural networks, and provides built-in on-device profiling tools to evaluate inference latency and memory footprint under realistic execution conditions. Experimental results demonstrate clear trade-offs between model complexity and deployability on a microcontroller, showing that classical models offer strong real-time performance while lightweight neural networks require careful resource management.
  Rather than proposing new learning architectures, the current work mainly focuses on system-level automation, deployability, and enabling researchers and developers to rapidly iterate on models and evaluate them directly on target hardware. Although demonstrated on the WeBe Band platform, the workflow is designed to be extensible to other ML-powered edge devices.

AI.tldr: An automated, hardware-aware edge ML workflow for the WeBe Band that integrates Piccolo AI to produce deployable, firmware-ready models with AutoML, quantization, and on-device profiling; classical models yield best real-time performance on microcontrollers, while lightweight NN require resource-aware management; extensible to other devices.
AI.motivation: Edge devices have strict compute and memory constraints, making ML development time-consuming and highly device-specific. There is a need for rapid, automated workflows that produce deployable, hardware-efficient models and firmware artifacts.
AI.method: An automated pipeline integrated with the Piccolo AI ecosystem to generate hardware-efficient models, including AutoML, hardware-aware quantization, and on-device profiling; generates deployable firmware artifacts and supports OTA deployment; supports multiple lightweight model classes (classical ML and neural networks) and real-time performance profiling.
AI.result: Experiments show trade-offs between model complexity and deployability on microcontrollers; classical models offer strong real-time performance, while lightweight neural networks require careful resource management to meet constraints.
AI.conclusion: Focus on system-level automation, deployability, and rapid iterative evaluation on target hardware; demonstrated on the WeBe Band and extensible to other ML-powered edge devices.

title: ASIRF: An Agentic Framework for Context-Dependent Sensitive Information Redaction
summary: Sensitive information is defined by domain and intent, not a universal category, yet redaction systems such as privacy filters and named-entity recognizers fix a taxonomy at training time, requiring retraining for each new domain. We introduce ASIRF (Agentic Sensitive Information Redaction Framework), which retrieves domain-specific definitions based on the input's domain from a flexible knowledge base at inference time, needing no retraining to adapt. Two architectures, a three-call multi-agent pipeline and a single-agent variant, are evaluated across ten small open-weight models and eight datasets, including out-of-distribution fictional domains, against the OpenAI Privacy Filter (OPF) as a trained-classifier baseline. With only a few dozen expert-authored definitions per domain and no training data, ASIRF's recall exceeds OPF's in 68 of 80 model-domain combinations (85 percent), by at least one of the two architectures, with shortfalls confined mostly to OPF's training-distribution domains.

AI.tldr: ASIRF introduces a domain-aware, retraining-free redaction framework that retrieves domain-specific definitions from a knowledge base at inference time, improving recall over a trained classifier baseline across multiple models and datasets.
AI.motivation: To overcome fixed taxonomy redaction systems that require retraining for every domain; enable flexible adaptation to new domains with minimal effort.
AI.method: Two architectures: a three-call multi-agent pipeline and a single-agent variant; leverage a knowledge base of expert-authored domain definitions; evaluate on ten open-weight models and eight datasets, including out-of-distribution fictional domains, compared to OpenAI Privacy Filter.
AI.result: ASIRF achieves higher recall than OPF in 68/80 model-domain pairs (85%), across both architectures; improvements evident with only dozens of domain definitions, no training data; shortfalls are mainly in OPF's training-domain domains.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-based, domain-informed redaction at inference enables robust cross-domain performance without retraining; provides flexible alternatives (two architectures) with strong recall; applicability extends to diverse domains with low data requirements; potential limitations include reliance on quality of the knowledge base and possible gaps for highly structured training domains.

title: From Text Decisions to Pixels: An Study of Jev-Style Visual Choice Model
summary: Visual software often needs a decision over supplied alternatives rather than a generated explanation. We present PixelJev, a native-image decision interface that maps an image, a task instruction, and a runtime candidate set to a structured choice and candidate-conditioned probabilities using small open multimodal models. Its initial realization unifies recognition and multiplechoice visual question answering through an existing language-model readout, with separately evaluated options for frozen inference, language-side adaptation, and held-out calibration. Across seven benchmark evaluations, 64-shot source adaptation raises Pets accuracy from 60.13% to 92.40% across optimization seeds and transfers to natural resampling, new texture labels, and A-OKVQA without target fitting, while frozen inference already supports both VQA tasks. A matched prompt-only follow-up on Pets and ScienceQA attributes the large Pets gain to adaptation and identifies a narrower output validity benefit of candidate readout in adapted VQA. Specialist DINOv2 probes remain stronger on source recognition, frozen 4B is stronger than adapted 2B on DTD and ScienceQA, and accuracy gains do not ensure calibrated target probabilities. These findings establish a working starting point for general-purpose visual decision models and identify the remaining requirements: schema robustness, cross-family transfer, and reliable use of visual evidence.

AI.tldr: PixelJev presents a native-image decision interface that maps an image, task instruction, and a runtime candidate set to a structured choice with candidate-conditioned probabilities, using small open multimodal models. It unifies recognition and VQA via a language-model readout and shows strong adaptation gains and calibration limitations across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: There is a need for decision-making over alternatives rather than generated explanations in visualAI, with a unified framework that supports recognition and VQA, while examining adaptation, calibration, and candidate-readout effects across datasets and model scales.
AI.method: The approach uses PixelJev, a native-image decision interface that combines image, instruction, and a runtime candidate set into a structured decision with probabilities conditioned on the candidate list. It leverages small open multimodal models with a language-model readout, and compares frozen inference, language-side adaptation, and held-out calibration. Evaluation spans seven benchmarks, including 64-shot source adaptation on Pets and transfers to natural resampling, new texture labels, and A-OKVQA without target fitting; includes a matched prompt-only follow-up and analyses of DINOv2 probes and model sizes (4B vs 2B).
AI.result: 64-shot adaptation raises Pets accuracy from 60.13% to 92.40% across seeds and transfers to several tasks without target fitting. Frozen inference already supports VQA tasks. Prompt-only analysis attributes large Pets gains to adaptation; identifies limited output validity benefits of candidate readout for adapted VQA. DINOv2 probes stay stronger on source recognition; frozen 4B outperforms adapted 2B on DTD and ScienceQA. Gains do not guarantee calibrated target probabilities.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a workable starting point for general-purpose visual decision models and highlights remaining needs: schema robustness, cross-family transfer, and reliable use of visual evidence.

title: RD-JEPA: Predictive latent pretraining for few-trajectory transfer across reaction--diffusion equations
summary: Learning surrogates for time-dependent partial differential equations often requires a new simulation corpus when the governing operator changes. We introduce RD-JEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture for self-supervised pretraining on reaction-diffusion trajectories. A single model is pretrained on five parameterized systems and then adapted to three held-out systems whose reaction operators and trajectories are excluded from pretraining. Using one, five, or ten complete trajectories from a held-out system, RD-JEPA achieves lower mean relative discrete $\ell^2$ field error and mean absolute spatial first-difference error than five supervised surrogate baselines, an independently trained control that removes the trajectory-dependent predictive latent pathway, and an architecture-matched model trained from scratch. Within the evaluated equations, output resolution, forecast horizons, and choices of adaptation trajectories, the results indicate that prediction of future-state representations can support data-efficient adaptation across related reaction-diffusion systems.

AI.tldr: RD-JEPA enables self-supervised pretraining across multiple reaction-diffusion systems and achieves data-efficient adaptation to held-out systems, outperforming supervised surrogates and scratch models across short-to-mid forecast horizons.
AI.motivation: Surrogates for time-dependent PDEs often require new simulation data when the governing operator changes; a transferable self-supervised framework can reduce data needs by learning representations that generalize across related reaction-diffusion systems.
AI.method: Pretrain a joint-embedding predictive architecture (RD-JEPA) on five parameterized reaction-diffusion systems. Adapt to three held-out systems whose reaction operators and trajectories were excluded from pretraining. Use 1, 5, or 10 trajectories for adaptation. Compare against five supervised surrogate baselines, an independently trained control that removes the trajectory-dependent predictive latent pathway, and an architecture-matched model trained from scratch.
AI.result: RD-JEPA achieves lower mean relative discrete L2 field error and lower mean absolute spatial first-difference error than baselines across evaluated settings. Adaptation is data-efficient (down to single-trajectory adaptation) and robust to variations in output resolution, forecast horizons, and adaptation trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Prediction of future-state representations via RD-JEPA enables data-efficient adaptation of surrogates to related reaction-diffusion systems and offers a competitive self-supervised pretraining approach compared to supervised surrogates and scratch models.

title: Evaluation of Multi-Turn Consistency in LLM Agents: Survival Analysis and Failure-Rationale Taxonomy
comment: Accepted at the ICLR 2026 Workshop on Logical Reasoning of Large Language Models
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents may perform well on isolated tasks yet drift into inconsistency over extended interaction. We evaluate temporal consistency in a controlled 20-step multi-agent setting inspired by delayed-gratification studies. At each step, an agent chooses between continuing to delay a reward or claiming it immediately (terminating the episode). Across a full-factorial manipulation of social visibility (private vs public), persona stressors, and deliberation policy, we run 84,540 trajectories spanning 8 model families.
